name: Biblical Chronology and Dating

objectives.text: Put pictures of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and Jesus in the order the Bible tells their stories
Describe the Bible as a true account of real events that took place over a very long time, from creation to Jesus
Explain from Galatians 4:4 that God sent his Son at the exact time he had planned
Place major Bible figures on a class timeline to show who lived before whom
Summarize the main eras of Old Testament history in order: creation, patriarchs, exodus and wilderness, judges, kings, exile, and return
Explain the meaning of BC, AD, BCE, and CE and why years before Christ count down while years after count up
Calculate the number of years between two dated events, including spans that cross from BC to AD with no year zero
Locate key anchor dates on a timeline, including David's reign, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and the return under Cyrus in 538 BC
Identify the ways the Bible itself marks time, such as regnal years, genealogies, and references to well-known events
Explain how dated promises and their fulfillment show the Reformed teaching that God governs real history according to his plan
Analyze the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 to explain how ages and the term fathered are used and why biblical genealogies may sometimes skip generations
Interpret the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 and explain how it is used to date the Exodus from Solomon's reign
Connect biblical events to dates fixed by outside records, such as the Battle of Carchemish in 605 BC and Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC
Compare the arguments for the early date and the late date of the Exodus, weighing the biblical numbers and archaeological evidence each side uses
Compare the 400 and 430 year time spans given for Israel's sojourn and explain the main proposals for reconciling them
Explain how archaeologists date ancient material through stratigraphy, pottery, inscriptions, and radiocarbon, and describe the limits of each method
Construct a synchronized timeline of the kings of Israel and Judah alongside Assyrian and Babylonian rulers using the cross-references in Kings
Analyze apparent conflicts in the regnal numbers of Kings by applying coregencies, accession and non-accession reckoning, and differing calendar years
Evaluate the differences among Masoretic, Septuagint, and Samaritan numbers in the Genesis genealogies and their effect on dating the flood and creation
Evaluate Ussher's chronology and other approaches to dating early Genesis, describing how Reformed interpreters have reasoned about the question
Analyze how prophetic time markers such as Jeremiah's seventy years relate to the dated events of the exile and return
Evaluate minimalist claims that the Israelite monarchy is not historical by weighing inscriptions such as the Tel Dan Stele, Mesha Stele, and Shishak's list against the biblical record
Produce a study tracing the Persian, Greek, Hasmonean, and Roman periods between the testaments and how they set the stage for Christ's coming

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (ordering figures, eras, BC/AD, genealogies, 1 Kings 6:1, fixed external dates, Exodus dating debate, synchronized king timeline, Masoretic vs Septuagint numbers, minimalism, intertestamental study). Merged the grade 6 calculation into a broader date-span skill that handles the BC to AD crossover. Turned the vague grade 1 and grade 3 timeline-string items into clear statements and expanded the eras list. Replaced the narrow David vs Exile comparison with placing anchor dates on a timeline. Added missing competencies: how Scripture marks time internally, God's providence over dated history, the 400 and 430 year spans, archaeological dating methods, coregencies and reckoning systems, Ussher and approaches to early Genesis chronology, and prophetic time markers such as the seventy years. Anchored objectives to specific verses and cited WCF 8.2, WCF 5.1, WSC Q11, and WCF 1.5 where they state the doctrine taught.
